summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised and has been lawful since 1832. The age of consent is 14 under Criminal Code article 308bis, with a three-year close-in-age exemption.

Article 14(II) of the 2009 Constitution, in force since February 2009, prohibits and punishes discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation, and guarantees equal recognition and exercise of rights.

The Law Against Racism and All Forms of Discrimination (Law 045), enacted on 8 October 2010, defines discrimination to include distinctions based on sex, sexual orientation and gender identity, and bars it in employment, services, education, health and other public and private spheres. It supplies definitions of transphobia, amends Penal Code article 281 to criminalise gender-identity-based discrimination, and makes dissemination and incitement punishable by one to five years' imprisonment. Since 2010, Penal Code article 40bis treats gender-identity motivation as an aggravating circumstance at sentencing.

The Gender Identity Law, passed by the Chamber of Deputies on 19 May 2016 and by the Chamber of Senators on 20 May 2016, signed on 21 May and in force from 1 August 2016, permits people over 18 to change name, sex and photograph on legal documents before the Civil Registry Service. The procedure is confidential, must be completed within 15 days, rests on a psychological test of voluntary assumption rather than surgery, and is reversible once. The first legal gender change under the law was recorded on 1 August 2016.

The changed sex marker is not recognised for marriage. In November 2017 the Supreme Court invalidated as unconstitutional a June 2017 Supreme Electoral Tribunal instruction to recognise it, and an appeal was lodged with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in May 2018.

Article 63 of the Constitution reserves marriage to heterosexual couples. Free unions between same-sex partners have been registered since 20 March 2023, when a Plurinational Constitutional Court ruling of 22 June 2022 obliging the Civil Registry Service to register them took effect; regulations were modified on 21 July 2023 to impose the same requirements and timelines as for heterosexual couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no access to marriage and depends on the free-union route for any recognition.

Single people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, and same-sex couples in a free union may adopt under article 84 of the Child and Adolescent Code.

Enforcement of the protection framework is weak. The Ombudsman reported in 2017 that only a minority of the murders of LGBT people recorded that year were investigated and that none produced a sentence. Reports of societal discrimination are common, and a 2024 national virtual survey, the first of its kind, documented widespread exclusion of LGBTI people.

A 2017 ILGA poll found 64% agreeing that transgender people should have the same rights, 63% that they should be protected from employment discrimination, and 53% that they should be able to change their legal gender.
tangentialFactors:
The armed forces announced in 2013 that LGBT citizens could serve from 2015, and transgender people serve openly. Reporting from 2014 described homosexuality in the military as taboo, with gay soldiers describing discrimination and sanctions only on condition of anonymity, and rights organisations pressing for openness; discretion in service is still advised.

The 2016 gender identity law passed despite low voter support for trans rights, carried by trans activists' access to legislators of the governing party. Heteronormative provisions were enacted alongside it because organised religion and LGBT organisations were both constituencies of that party.
localsOnly:
Name and marker changes are handled by the Civil Registry Service, which must process a request confidentially within 15 days on the basis of a psychological test of voluntary assumption. No surgical or medical evidence is required, and the change may be reversed once.

Free-union registration follows the same requirements and timelines as marriage for heterosexual couples after the July 2023 regulatory change. Fifteen couples had registered by January 2023 under Inter-American Court Advisory Opinion OC-24/17.

Adoption is open to single people regardless of sexual orientation and to same-sex couples in a free union under article 84 of the Child and Adolescent Code.

Men who have sex with men have been permitted to donate blood since 10 July 2019 under an amended Supreme Decree 24547, which replaced an earlier blanket ban that classed homosexual and bisexual men as a high-risk group.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources give conflicting dates for civil-union registration: one records civil-registry recognition in December 2020, while the court ruling that obliged registration is dated 22 June 2022 and took effect on 20 March 2023.

The outcome of the May 2018 appeal to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights on marriage recognition of a changed sex marker is not recorded in the sources.

The November 2015 government bill that became the Gender Identity Law was presented with an explicit exclusion of same-sex marriage; the sources do not describe any legislative change on that point beyond the 2017 Supreme Court ruling.

Official enforcement figures are limited to 2017 Ombudsman reporting; no more recent data on investigations or sentences appears in the sources.
